# AGENTS.md: working guide for `planet`

Rules for anyone writing code here, human or AI, whatever the agent. Every
`AGENTS.md`, here and in `apps/web` and `server`, has a `CLAUDE.md` symlink
beside it: edit only `AGENTS.md`. The block below is kb's, shared by the
studio's projects and in English; the rest is this project's and wins where
the two differ. `planet` is a codename; the name is pending (an open question).

<!-- kb:global · generated by kb gen -->
## Shared rules

Generated by `kb gen` from kb's templates: edit the template, not this block. The project section below wins where the two differ.

### Knowledge: one fact, one place

| Information | Home |
|---|---|
| current state (how it is) | the topic doc |
| why, and what was rejected | a decision: `kb decision new` |
| what will be done, in what order | the roadmap |
| an open question, or a problem without a chosen fix | an open question: `kb question add` |
| what changed, line by line | git |

A decision touches at most three places: the topic doc, the decision, and the roadmap or a question. Each says only its own fact and links to the others, all in the same commit as the change.

### kb: decisions, questions and docs

Decisions and open questions are one markdown file each, managed by `kb` (`bun kb --help`). Lists of them (indexes, the docs map, the sidebar, "decisions behind this page") are built when read, so nobody edits a list by hand and parallel branches never collide on one.

- **Before changing something, ask why it is so:** `kb why <doc.md#section | path>` and `kb search <terms>` show the current decisions, open questions and doc sections.
- **Record a decision** in the commit that makes it: `kb decision new "<title>" --decision "<what>" --why "<why>" --rejected "<options and why not>" --lives-in <doc.md#section>`. The title states the choice. Three to six lines in all.
- **Change of mind:** a new decision with `--supersedes <old id>` (or `--amends` when the old one stays partly true). The old file stays as the history of why; never rewrite it to say something else.
- **Open question** (for the client, for a specialist, or a problem without a chosen fix): `kb question add "<question>" --group <group> --owner <who> --unblocks "<what waits on it>" --context <doc.md#section>`, the day it comes up.
- **Answered:** `kb decision new ... --resolves <question id>` records the answer and closes the question; the new state goes into the topic doc.
- **References** are written from the docs folder (`billing.md#refunds`); a leading `/` is the repo root (`/scripts/deploy.ts`). Ids match by prefix or fragment.
- **`kb check`** before committing docs (CI runs it): broken links, missing anchors, stale generated blocks, references from code to docs that no longer exist. `kb gen` rewrites generated blocks and this block.
- Each topic doc carries frontmatter `title`, `group` and `summary`: they build the sidebar and the docs map.

### Writing: what is, in the present, affirmative

Applies to docs and code comments.

- Say what the thing is and what to do. A prohibition comes with the way: "never X; use Y".
- Present only. Docs and comments describe the system as it is today; the past lives in git (what) and in decisions (why). No "used to", "removed", "no longer".
- Changed or removed code: rewrite or delete, in the same commit, every comment and doc that talks about it. A comment about code that is gone misleads every model that reads it.
- Comments explain why; the code already says what.
- Concise: direct sentences, tables and lists when they fit. One file, one topic. Past ~200 lines (`kb check` warns), move a topic to its own doc, with its frontmatter; never summarize to fit, a summary loses facts.
- Notice the surroundings. Working on a piece, look around it: stale, duplicated, inconsistent or more complex than needed. Small and same topic: fix it in the same commit and say so. Bigger: point it out and propose, or record a question.

### Evidence before claims

- "Done", "fixed" and "passing" come after running the command in this turn and reading its output. Report the command and what it printed; a skipped step is reported as skipped.
- A visible change is looked at (screenshot or browser) before it is called done; tests prove only what they cover.
- Bug: reproduce it first, find the cause, then fix. A bug found in real use that earns a test gets one that fails on the old code before the fix makes it pass. After three fixes that did not hold, stop and question the approach instead of writing a fourth.
- Review feedback: check each point against the code before applying it, and answer with evidence when it is wrong. Agreement is not a reply.

### Thoughts that mean stop

| Thought | What to do |
|---|---|
| "I'll document it after" | Same commit, or it never happens. |
| "The decision is obvious, no need to record it" | If someone could ask "why?" in six months, record it. |
| "I'll update the list by hand" | Lists are built when read: use kb. |
| "Tests pass, so it works" | Look at it; tests prove what they cover. |
| "I know what the bug is" | Reproduce it first. |
| "This old paragraph is history, but useful" | History lives in git and decisions; the doc says what is. |
| "I'll keep this rule in my memory" | Rules every agent follows go in AGENTS.md; facts go in docs. |
| "It was only a question, but I'll fix it while I'm here" | Answer first; change when asked. |
| "It's a wip commit, I'll clean it later" | Later is the merge; retype or squash now. |

### Working with the person

- A feature that replaces a process the client already runs (spreadsheet, script, someone's routine): first a portrait of how it works today, validated with them; then a proposal in a separate document; the spec and the docs come after.
- A question gets an answer, the size of the question. Change something only when asked; when the answer shows a fix the person would obviously want, offer it in one line.
- Ask one question at a time, with your recommendation, when the choice is genuinely theirs; otherwise pick the conventional option, say so, and go on.
- Destructive or outward-facing actions (deleting data, pushing to a shared environment, sending messages) wait for an explicit yes.

### Commits

- Conventional Commits: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `chore`, `refactor`; the type drives the release (`feat` minor, `fix` patch, `BREAKING CHANGE` major). The project section says the language of the description.
- `wip` never reaches the integration branch: retype or squash before merging.
- Commits and pull requests end at their content: no `Co-Authored-By` trailer and no "Generated with" footer.

### Parallel agents: one worktree per feature

Several agents work at once, each feature in its own git worktree and branch; never two agents in one working directory.

- **Commit each green step** (tests and `kb check` pass) without waiting to be asked. Merging into the integration branch waits for the person's yes.
- **Show before merging:** the feature runs in its worktree and the person gets the URL to look at it (the project section says how).
- **Finish:** bring the integration branch in (`git merge <integration branch>`), resolve the conflicts yourself, run the checks and tests, then merge. Removing the worktree is the last step.
- **Talk before touching what another feature touches.** `herdr agent list` shows each agent and its worktree; `herdr agent prompt <pane> "<text>"` sends a message to any agent in a herdr pane (Claude, Codex, Kimi); `herdr agent read <pane>` shows its screen. Claude sessions also take SendMessage. Write as if the reader were another model: self-contained, with paths.
- A conflict that is not only yours (a business rule, the boundary between features) waits until both sides agree; never impose your version.
- Decisions and questions are one file each, so parallel branches add them without conflicts; shared lists are built when read.

# This project

- Why: [VISION.md](docs/VISION.md)
- Shape: [ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md); per theme,
  [WORLD.md](docs/WORLD.md), [RENDER.md](docs/RENDER.md), [PICTURES.md](docs/PICTURES.md),
  [SOUND.md](docs/SOUND.md), [PLUGINS.md](docs/PLUGINS.md) (how plugins speak) and
  [DEPLOY.md](docs/DEPLOY.md) (how an instance is hosted)
- The one current campaign: [BRIEF.md](docs/BRIEF.md); it dissolves when it ships
- Decisions and what was rejected: `docs/decisions/`, one file each
  (`bun kb decision list`, `bun kb search <terms>`)
- Next: [ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md). Unsettled, only there: `docs/questions/`
  (`bun kb question list`)
- Drawn ahead, nothing in it decided: the sketches in `docs/sketches/`
- Vocabulary: [GLOSSARY.md](docs/GLOSSARY.md). Use its terms, never invent synonyms
- Reference checkouts in `refs/`: [REFS.md](docs/REFS.md) says what may be taken

## Docs

- Homes, as the shared block says: the theme doc holds the state, a decision
  the why, ROADMAP what comes next, a question what has no answer. A change
  touches at most three: the theme doc, a decision, and ROADMAP **or** a question.
- Test first, write after: a step is built, shown running and tried by Marlus
  in the world before its docs are written. While it is refined, the commit's
  why is its record. When the shape has held: the theme doc, once, and a
  decision only for what is dear to undo.
- A decision is cited as `DECISIONS <fragment>`: the number the first entries
  carry (`DECISIONS 81`, or `(81)` in a doc's prose) or a piece of its slug.
  The fragment names exactly one file; `bun run docs` checks it. A new one
  takes a short slug: `bun kb decision new "<title>" --id <slug> ...`.
- Until a release carries what it decides, a decision is clay: rewritten in
  place as the design moves. Released, it is superseded or amended, never
  rewritten: `bun kb decision supersede <old> --by <new>`.
- A question's group is who or what it waits on: `marlus`, `hosting`,
  `plugins`, `building`, `later`, or `problems` for a problem with no chosen fix.
- Operational docs and the guides: titles and bullets, no prose, under 200
  lines (`bun run docs` fails over it). VISION, decisions and sketches keep
  prose: they carry the why and the what if.
- A struck ROADMAP item carries a decision's fragment, never the story.
  GLOSSARY updates in the change that adds, renames or shifts a term.
- No em dashes anywhere. English only: code, comments, docs, commits. Other
  languages appear only through i18n.
- `bun run docs` is `kb check`: kb's rules and this repo's own, held in
  `scripts/kb-plugins.ts` (`bun kb gen` rewrites the shared block). In `check` and CI.

## Sketches

- A sketch draws what may come, whole and far: where the seams lead, what the
  next plugins ask of the host. One file a subject, `docs/sketches/<subject>.md`.
- Its language is prose, the conditional, and ways side by side. Nothing in
  it is decided or built, and no code cites it.
- A piece leaves a sketch for a decision when a campaign pulls it. A sketch
  with nothing left to say is deleted.

## Craft (職人気質)

- Never the easy path: the cleanest, most long-term one, small core, sharp
  boundaries, cheap next change. "Works for now" is forbidden when a clean
  solution exists.
- If the clean path is more work: say so and do it. Never silently
  downgrade. "Start rough" means small scope, never low quality.
- A spike is how a design is tried: a branch `spike/<name>` or a crate of
  its own, rough on purpose, shown running, never merged. What lands is final.

## Who decides

- The session at work decides what can be undone, a shape, a seam, an order
  of work: it logs the choice as its own and shows it running. Marlus
  overturns it by seeing it.
- Marlus's alone, and worth a stop: the name, a licence, money, what is
  published, pushed or deleted, and what VISION says.
- An idea better than a logged decision is said beside the fragment it rewrites.

## Worktrees and other agents

- Worktrees are herdr's, most of the time: a session is born in one
  (`~/.herdr/worktrees/planet/worktree-<name>`, branch `worktree/<name>`), and
  a fresh one needs `bun install` before its first commit (the commit hook).
- The flow: commit each green step, merge into `dev`, close the worktree.
  Closing is herdr's too: `herdr worktree remove --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"`
  removes the folder and the workspace; `git branch -d <branch>` the branch.
  Outside herdr: `git worktree remove <folder>`.
- Several sessions may share one checkout. Before the first write: `git status`,
  `ListAgents` where the harness has it, one message naming your paths.
- A file another session is shaping is theirs: wait, then build on it. Read a
  shared file (this one, `scripts/`, the docs) right before editing it.
- Two sessions with the same task: tell the user and stop until one is named.
- Stage and commit only your own paths.

## What this is

- A finite, spherical world that people and AI agents walk, fly, drive and
  build in together: Cryptovoxels (voxels, building, land) + Hyperfy (GLB,
  entities, scripts). From scratch, free software end to end.
- One world per instance, hosted by mundos (`~/Dev/mundos`): it says who is
  who and addresses, versions and upgrades the world (DECISIONS 87).
- The core is what a world is made of and how it behaves; what is done with it is a plugin (DECISIONS 88, 106, 108).
- One Rust client (wgpu) on every screen: desktop, browser (WASM + WebGPU),
  Raspberry Pi, Quest, Pico. One Go server. The world is a recipe; the world
  folder holds only what someone changed. Offline mode is permanent.

## Layout

- `crates/`: Rust workspace, cut by dependency, not by platform.
  - `topology`: address, neighbours, sector seams, address <-> position.
    Pure integer logic where possible. No GPU, no IO.
  - `worldgen`: the generator. Deterministic; also built to WASM for the
    server. A world's shape is a source: plates over the seed, or a baked field.
  - `protocol`: wire messages generated from `proto/`; `lib.rs` alone by hand.
  - `scene`: the plain data a client hands a renderer. No GPU, no generator.
  - `avatar`: VRM avatars and humanoid clips: parse, retarget, pose. No GPU, no IO.
  - `voxel`: a volume's cells, gestures, sight, faces and footing. `vox`: a MagicaVoxel file as one grid, its palette and its faces. No sphere.
  - `part`: a placed thing that is no cell: its pose in the flat frame of its seat, its shape, what a line and a body meet of it. No sphere.
  - `seat`: how cells and parts are seated on a world, as client and server both hold it: plots, a volume's bounds by the ground, a gesture on the wire, the frame of a point and a part read back from the world.
  - `render`: all of wgpu lives here. `ui-native`: the desktop panel, all of egui.
  - `client`: controller, streaming, the cells, the host of plugins. No window, no DOM.
  - `plugins-client`, `plugins-world`: the version's plugins for each host, generated by `bun run plugins`.
  - `world`: what a plugin's world half stands on, their host, and the cells where the world is decided. `module`: its shell, the WASM file the server runs.
  - `shell-desktop` (winit), `shell-web` (wasm-bindgen), later `shell-xr`. `bench`: a frame's cost in WASM (`scripts/bench.ts`).
- `plugins/`: one folder a plugin: `world/`, `client/`, `wire/`, `web/` (docs/PLUGINS.md). Today: `chat`, `build`, `items`.
- `server/`: Go. The world server: one binary is an instance. Rules: `server/AGENTS.md`.
- `apps/web/`: Svelte + Bun, the web front end; hosts the WASM client. Rules: `apps/web/AGENTS.md`.
- `proto/`: the core's schemas, the wire and the module's bridge, single source for Rust and Go; a plugin's is in its folder; `bun run proto`.
- `assets/`: a version's default set and its `manifest.json`.
  `assets/fields/`: baked fields from `bun run field`, gitignored.
- `scripts/`: every repeated command. No tribal knowledge.
  `bun run setup | dev | server | web | wasm | assets | field | desktop | shot | webshot | bench | proto | plugins | module | kb | docs | check | build`.

## Invariants (expensive to get wrong)

- **Address is integer**: `(sector, u, v, h)` plus chunk and block index. The
  server is authoritative by address, never by float position.
- **Simulate flat, render spherical.** Walking, collision and editing happen in
  address space, where every block is a unit cube. World space is for
  rendering and for flight above the build band.
- **Camera-relative rendering.** No global f32 positions. Integer chunk
  coordinates + local float offset. Reversed-Z float depth.
- **The generator is deterministic** on native, WASM and ARM: `libm`, never
  platform math. Its version is frozen per world.
- **One read path**: `chunk(addr)` = stored chunk, else generated chunk.
  Callers never know which.
- **Copy on first write**: the first edit stores the whole chunk. The op log is
  append-only and records every edit, admins included.
- **Every edit is a permission-checked op** to the owner of what it changes,
  the core or one plugin (DECISIONS 93). Destruction is an edit.
- **Who is who is mundos's.** Accounts live there; the world checks a
  signature and keeps a level for the session's life.
- **A plugin imports the core**, never another plugin, and draws through
  `scene`. The core runs alone, with every plugin off.
- **A heavy file is named by the hash of its content.** Records name it so.
- **A person and an agent do the same things the same way** (DECISIONS 94),
  over one command/event seam: a front end is a UI on it, an agent a client
  with no renderer on the same protocol and levels. Tool logic lives in Rust.
- **Integrations enter through seams**, never through the core: one trait
  inside, library glue behind it in its own crate. No `cfg` sprawl.

## Performance (non-negotiable)

- Targets: a Raspberry Pi, a phone, a browser tab. Fast only natively is not fast.
- In the browser the generator, the streamer and the frame share a thread, and
  WASM costs several times native. Measure in WASM: `bun run bench` fails when
  a budget is blown.
- A change to `worldgen`, terrain streaming or per-frame client code runs
  `bun run bench` before it lands and says the numbers in the commit.
- Cost per sample is a design constraint, like determinism. What is the same
  for every sample is computed once in `Generator::new`, never per sample.
- A budget is raised only on purpose, with the why in a decision.

## Do NOT add

- Accounts, sign in, roles, a backoffice, a list of worlds, billing, a deploy
  to a box: they are mundos's (DECISIONS 87).
- Into the core, what a plugin can do. A hook waits for the plugin that asks.
- Bevy or any engine. Digging below the build band, multi-shell logic, flat
  or torus world types, structural collapse physics, our own transcoding.
- Code nothing pulls. The wish goes to ROADMAP, its drawing to a sketch.

## How it grows

- Draw ahead, build when pulled. A design is drawn whole and far in a
  sketch: where the host's seams lead, what a stranger's plugin needs. Code
  enters when the campaign in BRIEF.md pulls it, each step runnable.
  ROADMAP is intent, not contract: add wishes, reorder, strike with a decision.
- A feature is a plugin, and what the host offers plugins is the product:
  drawn as one API, cut piece by piece by the plugin that needs it, by
  extracting what exists (DECISIONS 88).
- Every change ends runnable and visible: headless render to PNG with a fixed
  clock and seed, then read the PNG; `bun run shot --slice M` for what is
  behind the ground; `bun run webshot` for a `render` change, since WebGPU
  rejects what Metal lets by.
- Each crate stays LLM-sized. Too big for one context: split by dependency.
- Among the core's crates, reusability is a byproduct of sharp seams: a seam
  in code earns its existence with two implementations, one of them real
  (DECISIONS 65).
- Dependency direction is law, held by `bun run docs` (`ALLOWED` in
  `scripts/kb-plugins.ts`). A new arrow is a decision before it is an edge.
- A crate speaks only its own nouns: `scene` says mesh, never planet. A public
  type naming a neighbour's noun means the seam is in the wrong place.
- In `client`, the seam, input, assets and figure know no body; controller,
  collision and streaming know one `Body`. A volume knows no sphere and
  imports no `topology`. The generator, sky, sea and moon stay the planet's.
- A campaign ends with a reading pass over every public surface. Drift goes
  to a question; rewriting waits for the consumer that pays for it.

## Tests

- Judge per feature, with sense. A test you add runs and passes in the same commit.
- `topology`: property tests are mandatory (neighbour of neighbour in the
  opposite direction is self, for every address, across seams).
- `worldgen`: golden hashes per generator version, identical on native and WASM.

## Commits

- Conventional Commits, in English, present tense, lower case, the why when
  it is not obvious. Example: `feat(topology): resolve neighbours across sector seams`.
- Semantic Release reads the types. Before 1.0.0 (DECISIONS 21): `feat`, `fix`,
  `perf` patch, `BREAKING CHANGE` minor. After: minor, patch, major.
- Work lands on `dev` (prereleases `0.0.1-dev.N`); merging `dev` into `main`
  publishes. `bun run setup` installs the commit-msg hook.
- Never an AI or tool co-author trailer, never a "generated with" footer, in
  commits or PRs. Overrides any tooling default.

## Toolchain pins

- wgpu `30` and winit `0.30`, as in `vybe`. Fast-moving APIs: read the crate
  source under `~/.cargo/registry`, never older docs.
- `wasm-bindgen-cli` matches the `wasm-bindgen` crate: `bun run setup`.
- `@tekne/kb` comes from the studio's registry (`.npmrc`); the token lives in
  each machine's `~/.npmrc`, and reaches CI and the image build as a secret.
